speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: Good day.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: It’s an honor, a true honor, to be back at the Federal Reserve and to take up this duty at a time of such consequence.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: I’ve been especially heartened by the warm welcome of old friends and new colleagues, both, and I’ve listened closely to my fellow FOMC members.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: I’ve heard a lot of new ideas, new thinking, and genuine interest in moving the Fed forward.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: This week’s FOMC meeting exemplified the very best of the Fed’s traditions: rigorous debate, open-mindedness, commitment to mission, responsibility, and accountability for performance.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: In this business, they all add up to one thing: getting monetary policy right—or as near to it as we can do.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: That is our North Star.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: My colleagues and I are here to serve our legislative remit, which you’ve heard us say before—price stability and maximum employment—and these objectives guided our business in the meeting just concluded.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: As you saw a few moments ago, the Committee decided to maintain the target range for the fed funds rate at 3½ to 3¾ percent, in support of the Fed’s dual mandate.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: The Committee also reaffirmed its policy of maintaining ample reserves in the banking system.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: Economic activity is expanding at a solid pace despite elevated uncertainty that owes, in part, to the conflict in the Middle East.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: Productivity growth and capital investment—both strong.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: Job gains have kept pace with the workforce, and the unemployment rate has changed little.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: We recognize that inflation has been running well ahead of the Fed’s long-stated inflation goal of 2 percent that’s been going on for more than five years.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: Persistently high prices are a burden for the American people.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: But the recent past need not be prologue.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: I am pleased to report that members of the FOMC are unambiguous and unanimous: This Committee will deliver price stability.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: At any institution, a change in leadership is a natural and timely opportunity to reaffirm its mission, to review current practices, and to consider whether those practices best meet our objectives.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: My Fed colleagues and I will be working in close collaboration to ask what changes might improve the conduct of monetary policy.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: On that score, you might have already noticed something: a difference in today’s policy statement.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: It’s a bit shorter, a bit simpler—and it dispenses with some older language.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: That statement just gives you the facts, as best we can judge it.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: Absent, also, is so-called forward guidance—which we agreed was not well suited to the current policy conjuncture.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: This afternoon, you also received the usual Summary of Economic Projections.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: It’s been the practice of this Committee for participants to submit these projections, and I have encouraged my colleagues to continue to do so.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: I, however, have refrained from offering any projections of my own, consistent with my long-held views on the SEP, at least as currently structured.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: In the median projections, real GDP rises at 2.2 percent this year, 2.3 percent next year, and total PCE inflation runs at 3.6 percent this year, 2.3 percent next year.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: The unemployment rate stands at about 4.3 percent.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: The median participant judges that the appropriate federal funds rate to be at 3.8 percent at the end of this year and 3.6 at the end of next.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: Let me turn now to a few words on a key initiative that we’re announcing today.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: I’m appointing a task force in each of five areas that are central to the broad conduct of monetary policy: First, Fed communications; second, the Fed’s balance sheet; third, our use and reliance on existing data sources; fourth, productivity and jobs in an era of transformation; and last, the Fed’s inflation frameworks.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: These subjects are timely, consequential, and, in my view, worthy of a fresh look.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: My colleagues and I discussed them with energy and purpose over the last couple of days.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: For each of these independent task forces, I’m enlisting some of the very best minds—both inside and outside the economics profession.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: They will be supported by subject matter specialists from our superb Fed staff.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: And they will have a straightforward charge: Start with first principles; ask hard questions; examine current practice; consider alternatives; and, ultimately, propose next steps for policymaker consideration.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: Since last summer, my colleagues discussed possible improvements in the form and function of Fed communications.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: This new task force will build on that effort and, I expect, propose some well-considered changes, including to the SEP I mentioned a few moments ago.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: The second task force, the one on balance sheet policy, will review the benefits and risks of the current ample-reserves regime and the composition of the Fed’s balance sheet.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: They will assess alternative frameworks for the conduct and operation of monetary policy.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: The third task force, the one on data, will evaluate new information sources and consider methodological changes to improve data gathering, with the aim of giving policymakers more accurate, relevant, contemporaneous, and, perhaps most important, actionable information on the state of our economy.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: Fourth, the task force on productivity and jobs.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: It’ll survey the pace, the reach, the economic impact of new general-purpose technologies, including AI, and explore the implications for the Fed in pursuit of our employment and inflation mandates.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: The last task force, the one on inflation frameworks, that’ll examine the drivers of inflation, first principles, and weigh the full range of ideas for delivering price stability in a changing economy.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: You’ll hear quite a bit more about these task forces and this overall initiative in the coming weeks.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: Enough for now to make a simple statement—each task force will serve an objective shared by everyone in the System, shared by everyone around that table that I sat with over the last couple of days: a Federal Reserve that is clear eyed about its mission, fit for purpose, and focused on the future.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: And with that, I appreciate your attention.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: I’m happy to take your questions.

speaker: MICHELLE SMITH
sentence: Howard Schneider.

speaker: HOWARD SCHNEIDER
sentence: Hi, Chairman.

speaker: HOWARD SCHNEIDER
sentence: Howard Schneider, with Reuters.

speaker: HOWARD SCHNEIDER
sentence: Good to see you again, and, and, and welcome back.

speaker: HOWARD SCHNEIDER
sentence: This is a lot to be putting in motion so fast.

speaker: HOWARD SCHNEIDER
sentence: What is the timeline you have in mind for, for each of these?

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: So I think it’ll depend on the task force and also depends on the urgency in which we need clear answers.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: My expectation—I’m still in the business of recruiting and finalizing them—my expectation is the task forces will begin work in the next couple of weeks, and we’ll start to get some more information from them, some more framing of how they see things starting in the fall, and hopefully most, if not all of them, concluding by year-end.

speaker: HOWARD SCHNEIDER
sentence: And just specifically on the inflation framework, you talk about first principles, does this include a review of the 2 percent target itself?

speaker: HOWARD SCHNEIDER
sentence: You’ve mentioned that things to the right of the decimal point don’t matter.

speaker: HOWARD SCHNEIDER
sentence: Should this be starting from a premise that 2 percent as a point estimate is, is too strict?

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: Let me break that into two pieces.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: First on the inflation framework review, their remit is, what are the drivers of inflation?

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: What’s the Fed’s responsibility for inflation?

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: In part, how do we measure inflation?

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: But that’ll overlap with my data group.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: On the 2 percent inflation objective, that is the Federal Reserve’s long-held objective of 2 percent.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: You’ve heard me say before, I tend to focus on the left of the decimal point.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: Well, the two is the left of the decimal point.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: For now, zero is to the right.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: I see no reason until we have reestablished our commitment and ability to deliver on the 2 percent inflation objective to revisit that.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: So that’ll be outside the scope of what we’re taking on.

speaker: MICHELLE SMITH
sentence: Colby.

speaker: COLBY SMITH
sentence: Thank you so much.

speaker: COLBY SMITH
sentence: Colby Smith with the New York Times.

speaker: COLBY SMITH
sentence: You’ve, in the past, said that inflation is a choice, and in the policy statement, it includes this pledge to deliver price stability, as you’ve reiterated today.

speaker: COLBY SMITH
sentence: But looking at the SEP, the bulk of your colleagues expect core PCE to run around 3.3 percent by year-end and for the 2 percent inflation target not to be reached until 2028.

speaker: COLBY SMITH
sentence: So I’m curious how patient you think the Fed can afford to be at this juncture in terms of waiting for one-time inflation waves to wash through and for underlying inflation to step down after so many years of inflation running above target?

speaker: COLBY SMITH
sentence: And under what circumstances you would support the Fed taking some action and raising rates?

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: Sure.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: So quite a bit there.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: Let me—let me try to break that into pieces.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: First, we have the capability and commitment to deliver on our price-stability objective of 2 percent.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: That’s exactly what we’re going to do.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: In the Fed’s review of its strategy over the last any number of years—in January, the Fed—including the strategy that we’re still bound by—the Fed statement says that inflation is primarily determined by monetary policy.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: You bet it is.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: I’ve said for years inflation is a choice.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: You bet it is.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: And today I’m announcing that this Committee, unambiguously and unanimously, have decided we are going to deliver on that.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: Rest of your question sounded like an encouragement for me to give forward guidance.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: We’ve dropped forward guidance.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: Some along the Committee I think dropped it, I suspect from our discussion the last couple of days, because they said, at this moment in time, it doesn’t feel as though providing forward guidance is right.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: Others have, I’d say, different views and think as a general proposition forward guidance isn’t the business we should be in.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: But that’ll be taken up by the task force on communications, and my policymaker colleagues, we’re going to listen hard to what the experts say and make our own decision.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: But I can’t give any forward guidance about what we’re going to do next.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: The good news is, we’ll be meeting in six weeks.

speaker: COLBY SMITH
sentence: So just following up, I guess on the current policy settings then, I am curious how restrictive you think things are at the current moment, given the flow of data that we’ve seen and, you know, forecasts that are coming down the pipeline.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: Yeah.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: I—I’ve heard characterizations, both inside in the Fed about that.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: I’ll give you my own.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: It’s uneven.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: And, if I look at the housing markets as one example, Fed policy isn’t the, the single determinant of the state of the housing market, but broadly I would say, there, Fed policy appears to be somewhat restrictive.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: I would have a hard time managing to say those words if I were to see what’s happening in financial markets, so I’d say it’s uneven.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: That’s perhaps a function of different transmission mechanisms of monetary policy, whether monetary policy is coming from our interest rate tool or our balance sheet tool.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: But the good news, we have a task force on that, too, and the balance sheet task force will be looking more at that subject.

speaker: MICHELLE SMITH
sentence: Mike McKee.

speaker: MICHAEL MCKEE
sentence: You’ve said you, you don’t like forward guidance.

speaker: MICHAEL MCKEE
sentence: You dropped it from the statement this time.

speaker: MICHAEL MCKEE
sentence: But with the dot plot, nine members suggested that they want a rate increase by the end of the year, and the markets have taken that as forward guidance.

speaker: MICHAEL MCKEE
sentence: So what does this mean in terms of how you guide the markets and in terms of what the dot plot’s future is?

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: I’m going to have to give you the same answer I gave to, to Ms. Smith; we’ve got a task force for that.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: I’ll give you a little bit more.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: I reviewed the dot plots, and when I saw the submissions, I noted that all the submissions were coming in with pencils, you know those kinds with the big erasers.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: That’s to say that I think my colleagues around the table, when they submitted their dots, understand the world is changing quite quickly.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: And they didn’t feel bound by them six weeks from now or six days from now and if—in the event that their circumstances change.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: I’ll note a couple other things.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: What I heard around the table was, as they submitted their modal forecasts, their modal forecasts—to be clear—weren’t, this was more likely than not.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: This was—this was more likely than their other scenarios.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: So I didn’t hear tons of conviction.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: What I heard was the kind of humility that I think we should have.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: I did not submit a, a dot.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: For me, it’s not helpful in the conduct of policy.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: I suspect, by year-end, as I mentioned in my opening statements, there’ll be a review about communications broadly, press conferences, dots, meetings, and the like, transcripts, minutes.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: This will be part of that.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: I don’t want to prejudge the outcomes there, but I’m pretty open minded about what they could be.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: And I was just incredibly impressed over the last couple of days.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: My colleagues over the last two days, and frankly, over the first three weeks I’ve been here, they’ve been very open about changes.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: Change isn’t easy.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: Change is filled with risk.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: But our number one goal is to get monetary policy right.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: The way to get monetary policy right is to deliver on the remit that Congress gave us to deliver on price stability.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: And there was no disagreement on any of those points.

speaker: MICHAEL MCKEE
sentence: At the risk of possibly getting the same answer about task forces, communications, what is your feeling about these news conferences?

speaker: MICHAEL MCKEE
sentence: Are you going to continue one after every meeting?

speaker: MICHAEL MCKEE
sentence: Do you think—find them useful?

speaker: MICHAEL MCKEE
sentence: What is the future for the way Kevin Warsh will communicate?

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: Well, this one’s probably got another 15 or 20 minutes in it, so I don’t want to prejudge the outcome.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: Press conferences can be a very useful way to communicate with households, businesses, and more broadly, through using the likes of you.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: I had a great old mentor named George Shultz, and his mantra was, “Press conferences are useful.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: But when you have one, you want to make sure you have something important to say.” Today I think we had something important to say about our commitment to deliver on price stability, our commitment to rethink practices with an eye of moving the Fed forward, and to give you and the American people a sense that these aren’t idle thoughts.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: These are concrete thoughts that we’re going to seek out the best minds, both the best thinking inside of the Federal Reserve and the best people I know in business, and economics, and the academy, and technology, and the rest, to share their views.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: That’s what we’re going to be doing here, the pursuit of truth.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: I think we’re going to come up with some new and interesting things.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: We made some changes today.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: I expect more changes to come, and, and some of those might well be worthy of a press conference.

speaker: MICHELLE SMITH
sentence: Chris Rugaber.

speaker: CHRIS RUGABER
sentence: Hi.

speaker: CHRIS RUGABER
sentence: Chris Rugaber at Associated Press.

speaker: CHRIS RUGABER
sentence: Thanks for taking our questions.

speaker: CHRIS RUGABER
sentence: Could you give us a sense of how you see inflation more in the long term?

speaker: CHRIS RUGABER
sentence: I know you may not want to comment on the ups and downs.

speaker: CHRIS RUGABER
sentence: But is this mainly driven by energy prices and the Iran war at this point, or do you have any concerns about underlying inflation pressures in the economy?

speaker: CHRIS RUGABER
sentence: Thank you.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: So I can’t do much better than, than the Committee just did, so let me—let me restate it.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: Inflation remains elevated relative to the Committee’s 2 percent goal, in part reflecting supply shocks that have driven price increases in certain sectors, including energy.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: That paragraph goes on to say, but to be clear, the Fed’ll deliver price stability.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: My own judgment is the Committee spent quite a bit of time, not just in two days but over iterations of a couple weeks.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: That’s what we’re prepared to say about inflation, but the commitment to deliver is strong, unanimous, and unambiguous.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: And that’s, I think, an important message we’ve missed for five years, and, and we’re going to fix that.

speaker: CHRIS RUGABER
sentence: Well, great.

speaker: CHRIS RUGABER
sentence: And then just on your—the, the data task force and everything else, I mean, generally speaking, I think people feel the—feel the Fed looks at everything already, certainly that was the sense from before.

speaker: CHRIS RUGABER
sentence: What’s—is there data that you feel is not given enough weight?

speaker: CHRIS RUGABER
sentence: I mean, you mentioned the trimmed mean in the past, but again, that’s well known to certainly most Fed members.

speaker: CHRIS RUGABER
sentence: So what is that task force looking at and, and what, what might be the—I mean, I know you don’t want to prejudge the outcome, but are there examples of data that you expect might be given more weight?

speaker: CHRIS RUGABER
sentence: Thank you.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: So you’re answering my question.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: So let me say, I don’t want to prejudge the outcome.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: I also don’t want to say too much about what they’re going to do because I still have a phone call or two to make before I’ve nailed down the people that are doing that.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: I’m interested [in] what the outside experts’ view is on the subject.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: I’ll say this generally: Most of the data that central bankers and other government officials in the United States consume come with old-fashioned survey methods, national accounts of what the U.S. economy looks like that looks very little like the U.S. economy in 2026, survey methods that don’t have response rates that we need, asking questions that might’ve been quite applicable a generation ago that are less applicable now.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: So even inside of official statistics, I would be open minded if the task force and our own best thinking had recommendations how those official statistics can be brought up to a standard of, of our time using new analytic methods.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: I’d also say this: Almost every private company CEO that’s running his or her business are doing so with real-time information that isn’t subject to much revision, that is telling them what just happened at that very moment.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: As you know, there are normal long and variable lags in the conduct of monetary policy.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: What we’re really interested in is what’s happening right now.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: What we’re less interested in is echoes of history.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: And you’re hearing from my answer that some of the data that we receive, that we’re waiting on, the first Friday after the month, the payroll index, or something else, that might be an echo of history that’s quite useful on its third revision.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: We need to take those error bounds down because we have to make hard decisions in real time.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: I’m really open minded that there is a lot of new data sources that we can learn from the private sector, from reforms in the official sector, and new analytic techniques that are far more refined than asking a simple question about whether something was core or noncore.

speaker: MICHELLE SMITH
sentence: Edward.

speaker: EDWARD LAWRENCE
sentence: Thanks.

speaker: EDWARD LAWRENCE
sentence: Welcome, Mr. Chairman.

speaker: EDWARD LAWRENCE
sentence: Edward Lawrence with Fox Business.

speaker: EDWARD LAWRENCE
sentence: So, if you don’t give a lot of ongoing forward guidance, won’t the markets have more volatility?

speaker: EDWARD LAWRENCE
sentence: And shouldn’t Americans have more access into what you’re thinking going forward?

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: So I think financial markets perform best when they react to incoming data.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: I think they—the financial markets work less efficiently when they ask a question: How will the Federal Reserve react to that incoming information?

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: The more that markets are paying attention to what’s happening in the real economy, deciding what’s good data and what’s less good data, the more financial markets can price what they believe is the most likely and what are the tail risks.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: Financial market prices are probably the most important source of information to guide central bankers.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: But when all the financial markets are doing is reflecting back what we’ve said, then we’re taking the most important source of information and we’re being blind to it.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: I’d like us to create a system where those blinders come off, where markets are following data that they efficiently think is reliable.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: And they’ll be watching data.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: We’ll be watching data.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: They’ll come with better information through market prices to us.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: We can make more informed decisions.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: But ultimately, the goal that I said at the outset, deliver on the price-stability objective that Congress told us to do and that we’ve got to get in the business of doing.

speaker: EDWARD LAWRENCE
sentence: If I could take you in the meeting a little bit.

speaker: EDWARD LAWRENCE
sentence: So your first meeting, the, the Board members seemed fairly hawkish when you listen to—in general, when you listen to what they’re saying.

speaker: EDWARD LAWRENCE
sentence: Was there any discussion of a rate cut going forward today?

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: There was one proposal on the table.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: There was no discussion of any other proposals.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: The discussion on that proposal, I would say, was quite limited.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: The group was unanimous and unambiguous on it.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: It has been the practice of this central bank and others to have a range of alternatives.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: Today we had one.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: I thought it furthered discussion, deepened it and made it clear what we needed to do and how we need to deliver.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: I wouldn’t prejudge what happens in the future, but there was only one big subject for us.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: We took it on.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: We had a good family fight on it for a couple of days, and we ended up, I think, in a better place.

speaker: MICHELLE SMITH
sentence: Claire.

speaker: CLAIRE JONES
sentence: Thanks a lot.

speaker: CLAIRE JONES
sentence: Claire Jones, Financial Times.

speaker: CLAIRE JONES
sentence: You know, coming to this “blind,” reading this very nice, short statement that I think we’ve all appreciated in the room, one might wonder why you didn’t raise rates today considering what you’re saying here about the, the risks to U.S. inflation and your mandate.

speaker: CLAIRE JONES
sentence: I guess why not and what would you need to see in order to get to that place?

speaker: CLAIRE JONES
sentence: And secondly, on your task forces, are there any best practices of the central banks that you’d consider looking at?

speaker: CLAIRE JONES
sentence: Thank you.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: Yeah.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: I’m glad they’re in the practice of giving you two questions, because my answer to your first question was to be very curt.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: I’ve got nothing more to say than the statement itself.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: And to the point of the question I got before: Market reactions to what we say, unfiltered, I think is more helpful than, having delivered a statement, me then improvising further upon it.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: Best practices of task forces, this is a subject I’ve thought some about.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: I’ve been on a task force or two in my life.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: Best practice, find the best minds.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: Ensure that the task forces have a range of people, both by backgrounds and predispositions, so they, too, can have a bit of a family fight.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: Make sure when you establish a task force that the group that’s going to be the recipient of the information feels as if they’ve got some equities in it, too.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: That’s why we’re looking for—haven’t done the final roll call—some of the most significant talent we have in the building and across the Reserve Banks on each of these and, in some sense, seconding them to this group for a period of some number of months so that the leaders of the task force know what the most analytical central bank in the world thinks about that.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: They can reflect on it.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: And a final best practice, we’re not outsourcing decisions to anybody.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: Administrations past and present, Reserve Banks have chosen a group of 19 people around the table.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: These will be our decisions.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: We can agree to some of the recommendations, disagree with others, have a good family fight about it.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: But what comes from them will, I hope and believe, make the discussion we have internally better, stronger, more of a dialectic, so that we can finally deliver on that price-stability objective.

speaker: CLAIRE JONES
sentence: Just a quick follow-up on your, your markets’ point, if you look at two-year yields, they’re really suggesting that markets think more tightening is needed.

speaker: CLAIRE JONES
sentence: Would that be your read on what the two-year yield is saying as well?

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: We were in such a good place.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: This is why we don’t do third questions, I presume.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: I’m not going to offer any commentary on market reaction over the last 30 or 60 minutes.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: What we’ve given markets is a new chapter for the central bank, some fresh thinking.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: What we’ve given markets, and households, and businesses, I think, is a commitment to ask ourselves hard questions, such that we can deliver on the promises that we’ve made before.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: This is a lot of change for financial markets to digest.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: I wouldn’t be particularly intrigued by how they react in the first several minutes or even first several days.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: What I think is most important is that financial markets, and at least as important, households and businesses, know that the central bank will deliver on price stability.

speaker: MICHELLE SMITH
sentence: Brian.

speaker: BRIAN CHEUNG
sentence: Hi, Chairman Warsh.

speaker: BRIAN CHEUNG
sentence: Brian Cheung with NBC News.

speaker: BRIAN CHEUNG
sentence: Thank you for taking our questions.

speaker: BRIAN CHEUNG
sentence: So, when you say that we’ve dropped forward guidance, for the layperson, that might sound like the Fed’s going to say less or offer less insight into where their borrowing costs might go.

speaker: BRIAN CHEUNG
sentence: So, for the person that maybe you might run into at the grocery store, where the price tags are rising at a faster pace than their wages at the moment, how would you explain it to them?

speaker: BRIAN CHEUNG
sentence: I don’t know if “task force” might be the answer there, but how would you kind of communicate this era, this chapter of the Fed?

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: If I told somebody in the milk aisle that I had a task force for that, I think that would be doing a very poor job, so I appreciate it.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: If I saw somebody in the grocery store, what I would say to them is that we cannot have a very significant effect on particular prices.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: The price of oil in the markets today or even the price of a dozen eggs, that does not have first-order consequences to what we’re doing.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: But we do have a really important job there, and it’s to make sure that those changes in oil, or beef, or eggs, or milk don’t broaden in the economy, don’t have second- and third-order effects.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: That’s our job.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: That’s our commitment.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: That’s our capability, and we’re going to deliver on it.

speaker: BRIAN CHEUNG
sentence: And then is the Fed’s relationship with the Treasury also under review?

speaker: BRIAN CHEUNG
sentence: There was the normal breakfast meetings with the Treasury Secretary.

speaker: BRIAN CHEUNG
sentence: Is that something you intend to continue doing, and have you had conversations with the President since your swearing in?

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: So, on the President, I, I don’t have anything for you.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: With respect to the Treasury Secretary, he has been posting pictures of our breakfasts, so I don’t think I can—I don’t think I can deny that.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: The long tradition at the central bank is that the Fed Chairman and the Treasury Secretary meet weekly.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: I think we’ve pulled off three of those so far.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: I believe he’s overseas this week, so this’ll be the exception to the rule.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: I think they’re very useful discussions.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: The central bank’s objectives and our roles and responsibilities are quite delineated from the fiscal authorities.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: And, in my view, monetary policy is independent in the conduct of what we do, but that doesn’t mean we’re not interested in what’s happening with the fiscal authorities.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: The way I think about it is this central bank needs to have a wide lens but a narrower remit.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: We need to be quite interested in what’s happening in the world.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: I won’t be breaking any news here to suggest that I’m quite interested what’s happening in the Middle East.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: That does have some effect on our day job.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: It doesn’t mean it’s our responsibility, but I think we’re going to keep a wide lens.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: And my meetings with Secretary Bessent to this point have helped widen that aperture.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: So we’re aware of things that could affect our day job, even if it isn’t.

speaker: MICHELLE SMITH
sentence: Steve.

speaker: STEVE LIESMAN
sentence: Steve Liesman, CNBC.

speaker: STEVE LIESMAN
sentence: Mr. Chair—Mr.

speaker: STEVE LIESMAN
sentence: Chairman, thank you for taking my question.

speaker: STEVE LIESMAN
sentence: You had said in the—before you became Chairman that you thought productivity was a reason why the Federal Reserve could lower interest rates.

speaker: STEVE LIESMAN
sentence: Do you still believe that to be the case?

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: So the Committee had a discussion of productivity today.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: AI came up.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: The way I thought about it before and socialized with the group is that artificial intelligence, the latest generation of general purpose technology, is perhaps as important a change in the economy and business and households that we’ve had in my adult lifetime.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: It is filled with both a huge opportunity and with risks.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: I take both of those very seriously.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: You may have heard me say before that AI is shorthand perhaps for American ingenuity.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: That doesn’t mean that it’s going to be easy.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: That certainly doesn’t mean it’s not going to be disruptive.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: But over the long term, my conviction—and I heard quite a bit of support for this around the Committee today—is the United States is a winner as we go down this.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: The United States is ultimately going to be better off in that.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: Now, to bring that back to the conduct of policy, timing, scale, speed, implications for output and employment, it’s one of the things we have a task force to do.

speaker: STEVE LIESMAN
sentence: [Laughter] If you don’t mind a follow-up from the other side, which is that, when you look at the strong job growth that’s out there, the elevated inflation, GDP seems to be going pretty good and the stock market seems to be soaring, do you look around this economy and see the funds rate being restrictive?

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: So that’s your second question.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: I’m going to give the same answer that I gave before.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: I’d say, as I think about the conduct of policy, what matters is what’s the effect of policy, not what do we say, but what happens.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: And the best way I can describe is, it’s uneven.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: I do see some restrictiveness on things like housing.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: It’s hard to use those same words anywhere else.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: I’ll just make one other point.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: You talked about one of our dual mandates and the employment side.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: I don’t believe that we have a cruel choice.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: I don’t share the view that was expressed a few generations ago that Federal Reserve chairmen show up a podium like this and say, “You’ve got to choose.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: And you’re going to have to decide whether you’re willing to tolerate higher inflation to put more people at work.” I don’t believe in that.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: What I believe is, if we do our job, we can make strong growth, low prices, and strong employment mutually compatible.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: And so what you heard from the Committee today is, we’ve got some work to do on this price-stability front.

speaker: MICHELLE SMITH
sentence: Nick.

speaker: NICK TIMIRAOS
sentence: Thank you.

speaker: NICK TIMIRAOS
sentence: Nick Timiraos with Wall Street Journal.

speaker: NICK TIMIRAOS
sentence: Chairman Warsh, you’ve said repeatedly credibility is earned by delivering.

speaker: NICK TIMIRAOS
sentence: If credibility requires delivering, the move would be to tighten or at least to threaten to.

speaker: NICK TIMIRAOS
sentence: Now, you didn’t do that today.

speaker: NICK TIMIRAOS
sentence: Why not?

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: That judgment you expressed was not expressed by any of the 19 people around the table.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: We’ll be meeting in six weeks, and we’ll take up the issue again.

speaker: NICK TIMIRAOS
sentence: And, and, if I could ask about AI, the buildout is generating enormous demand right now, cap-ex, data centers, power.

speaker: NICK TIMIRAOS
sentence: The productivity payoff may be further out.

speaker: NICK TIMIRAOS
sentence: So, in your judgment today, is AI adding more to demand or to supply?

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: It’s a good question.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: At the central bank and in the economics profession, what we spend most of our time doing is counting demand.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: It’s easier.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: We can see it.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: We can count it.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: We can check it.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: We can revise it.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: What we do, though, is we infer supply.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: You’ll notice in the second paragraph of what one of your colleagues described as “a very short statement,” we have a sentence on the demand side and a sentence about the same length on the supply side.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: They’re both important.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: Just because we can count one better than the other doesn’t mean we’re going to favor one more than the other.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: With respect to AI and the growth of data centers and infrastructure around it, we’re counting the demand side, and it is no doubt showing up in GDP figures.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: We can be less certain when we infer the timing and extent of the growth on the supply side.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: It may well be an intuition the supply side is going to expand, but it’ll take longer.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: But just describe it this way: There’s a race between supply and demand.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: Milton Friedman says that the only thing we know about economics is that there’s a supply line and a demand line and they ultimately cross.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: When they cross, what are the implications for policy?

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: The good news for you is, we have a task force for that.

speaker: MICHELLE SMITH
sentence: Andrew.

speaker: ANDREW ACKERMAN
sentence: Thanks, Mr. Chairman.

speaker: ANDREW ACKERMAN
sentence: It sounded like on the task force on data that, that you were looking at overhauling or completely overhauling the system of national accounts, the way that government monitors the economy.

speaker: ANDREW ACKERMAN
sentence: Is that your ambition?

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: In a word, no.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: In a few words, much of this data gathering happens in other government agencies to which we owe a tremendous amount of respect, a tremendous amount of deference.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: But, if in the course of this, we come up with recommendations, which Fed staff have already begun to develop, about things that they could be doing to help inform us as policymakers, we’re not going to hesitate.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: Again, I don’t want to try to delineate the four corners of the research of the task force on data, but I do think there will be a review of official statistics, and at least as important, a view of bringing the best practices from the private sector and new analytical tools made possible by AI, so we can forge these into a fabric that gives us better real-time information.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: So, as I mentioned before, when we’re making decisions, we’re making decisions that we’d say are real contemporaneous data, not data that we call “contemporaneous.” It’s really an echo of history.

speaker: ANDREW ACKERMAN
sentence: Okay.

speaker: ANDREW ACKERMAN
sentence: Thanks.

speaker: ANDREW ACKERMAN
sentence: The other question I wanted to ask is related to the building renovations.

speaker: ANDREW ACKERMAN
sentence: Are you considering any changes to the renovations, the projects, just in light of the fact that they became kind of a political football in the last year?

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: I heard something about that.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: I don’t think I’m breaking any news, but my view is, when you show up at a new institution, you should go meet with the Inspector General, just as a matter of good practice.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: It’s a practice that I hope to continue.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: I’ve had one meeting with the Inspector General, and he told me what I believe the world knows, which he’ll be coming out with a report on the building and the building projects at some point later this summer.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: And I’ll be interested in reading the report.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: From my perspective, with a forward-looking glance, is there anything that we can be doing or should be doing from this moment until the completion of the project to do what we can to be good stewards of taxpayer money and make sure that we’re delivering on the promises that we made?

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: So more work to do.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: You might not be surprised, in the first few weeks, I’ve been somewhat preoccupied on other matters, but I promise to, to get to the full breadth of the Fed’s tasks in the weeks ahead.

speaker: MICHELLE SMITH
sentence: Victoria.

speaker: VICTORIA GUIDA
sentence: Hi, Victoria Guida with Politico.

speaker: VICTORIA GUIDA
sentence: So I know that you did not submit a forecast, but you are the person who is authorized to speak on behalf of the FOMC.

speaker: VICTORIA GUIDA
sentence: So I’m wondering if you could tell us, in the SEP, the increase in the expectations for inflation, is that all because of the Iran war?

speaker: VICTORIA GUIDA
sentence: What was the discussion around what—the expectations for inflation being higher and also potentially growth being slower?

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: So my read of what I heard in the room reflected, I must admit, in the SEPs, is half of my colleagues thought the policy rate, given all those developments, should be at this level or lower between now and year-end and the other half thought higher.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: That 19th voter was me, and I didn’t submit one.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: There’s a range of views on the questions of first- and second-round effects, no resolution or conviction.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: But we’ll be meeting again in six weeks.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: I think we’re going to know more then.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: And I think that my colleagues are very attentive to incoming developments between now and then.

speaker: VICTORIA GUIDA
sentence: And can I just—quick follow-up on the SEP?

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: Sure.

speaker: VICTORIA GUIDA
sentence: You said that you’re still encouraging your, your fellow Committee members to submit forecasts, even if you’re not doing it.

speaker: VICTORIA GUIDA
sentence: So what do you think is the benefit of them doing it even if you don’t?

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: That’s the commitment that the FOMC made, and it’s a commitment that I hope we live up to.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: Commitment we made was to deliver price stability.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: I expect us to live up to it.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: By the time we get to the end of this year, as I mentioned, I wouldn’t be surprised if there was a new communications framework, there were some changes to the SEP. That’s a Committee discussion, a robust discussion, and I think we’ll have it.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: I believe we’re going to come to a better mix of communications to deliver on what we promised, but I wouldn’t want to prejudge what those are.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: But between now and then, I would continue to expect colleagues to submit their SEPs.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: Some of them I think believe that the practice as currently structured is okay.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: But I heard a lot of interest in real reform, generally about all of these topics.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: You didn’t ask it, but I’ll answer.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: It was a pretty gracious couple of days, and it’s been a pretty warm few weeks.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: The institution wants to figure out how we can do better.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: The institution’s going back to first principles.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: And I’m encouraged that what we’ve done in the statement, what we’re thinking about doing with respect to the SEP, that instinct towards a new chapter is a real one.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: And by the end of the year, I hope we can put some points on the board both in form and in substance of delivering.

speaker: MICHELLE SMITH
sentence: Go to Enda for the last question.

speaker: ENDA CURRAN
sentence: Thank you, Mr. Chairman.

speaker: ENDA CURRAN
sentence: Enda Curran, Bloomberg News.

speaker: ENDA CURRAN
sentence: Could you guide us through, please, some of the principles that guide your own reaction function, and tell us a little bit about kind of conditions that you think when the Fed should respond.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: It’s going to be a very unsatisfactory answer to the final question.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: The Federal Reserve has a lot of responsibilities, not just in monetary policy, but in supervision and regulation, consumer affairs, and payments.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: My own view is our credibility comes from delivering on what we’re saying we’re going to do across everything we do.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: I’ve devoted more time in my first three weeks to monetary policy than all those things.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: But the more we deliver on our promises as good supervisors and good regulators, the more benefit we get, the more credibility enhancement we have in monetary policy.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: When we deliver on our price-stability objectives, which we will, the American people will feel as though the hardships that they’ve been living through, in part because of inflation in the last five years, are in the rearview mirror, and that credibility will have dividends, dividends across what we do.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: And the institution will come to press conferences like this always with an impetus to reform, always with an impetus to, to do better.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: But we’re going to put some points on the board.

speaker: ENDA CURRAN
sentence: Can I ask you about the labor data in recent months?

speaker: ENDA CURRAN
sentence: How would you sum up labor data—labor market right now, do you see it as stable, or as potentially a source of inflation?

speaker: ENDA CURRAN
sentence: Thank you.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: Yeah.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: So, so the Committee—if I were to try to capture how the Committee thought about it, the Committee thought that the labor markets were stable.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: There were some people around the Committee who thought that it was trending better than that.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: Trends matter more than data points.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: What’s happening over three or six months matters more than any one data point—any one data release.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: And I’d say the jobs data’s been moving in a good direction.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: If I heard one other thing around that subject over the course of the last couple of days, what I heard was that strong productivity-led growth is not something that we fear, but something we embrace.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: Thank you all very much.
